subChunks.title: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
subChunks.hookHtml: ACID is the contract a database makes with you. Break it — or use a system that does not guarantee it — and you get corrupted data under concurrent load.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Atomicity

A transaction is all-or-nothing. If any statement fails, all changes are rolled back. You never observe a half-completed transaction.

Failure without atomicity: debit Alice, system crashes, credit Bob never happens. XP disappears.

Consistency

Every transaction moves the database from one valid state to another. Constraints (NOT NULL, CHECK, FK) are enforced at commit time. A transaction that would violate a constraint is rolled back.

Isolation

Concurrent transactions should not interfere with each other. The degree of isolation is configurable (isolation levels — next lesson). Without isolation, two concurrent reads of the same balance followed by two writes can double-credit or double-debit.

Classic concurrency bugs without isolation:

  • Dirty read — reading uncommitted changes from another transaction
  • Non-repeatable read — two reads in the same transaction return different values because another transaction committed in between
  • Phantom read — a range query returns different rows on second execution because another transaction inserted new rows

Durability

Once COMMIT is acknowledged, the data is on disk (write-ahead log). A server crash after COMMIT does not lose the transaction. PostgreSQL achieves this via WAL (Write-Ahead Log).

BASE vs ACID

NoSQL systems often offer BASE (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent) instead of ACID. BASE trades strong consistency for availability and partition tolerance. Understanding the difference helps you choose the right database for the job.

storyBeats.text: The payment processor crashes mid-transaction. When the server restarts, XP has been subtracted but never awarded.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Atomicity says: the entire transaction commits or nothing does. Consistency says: constraints are always satisfied. Isolation says: concurrent transactions do not corrupt each other. Durability says: a committed transaction survives a crash. These are the four pillars. Remove any one and the archive eventually lies.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 ACID scenario analysis

For each scenario, identify which ACID property was violated:

  1. Two concurrent transactions both read balance=100, both add 50, both write 150 back — the actual balance should be 200.
  2. A transfer succeeds (debit + credit both execute) but after a server crash the credit is gone.
  3. An INSERT violates a NOT NULL constraint but the transaction commits anyway with a NULL in the column.
  4. Transaction A reads a row; Transaction B updates and commits it; Transaction A reads the same row again and sees the new value within the same transaction.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Isolation violated — the lost update problem. Both transactions read the same initial value and overwrite each other's result. Proper isolation (e.g. SERIALIZABLE or SELECT FOR UPDATE) prevents this.

2. Durability violated — the committed transaction was lost on crash. Properly durable databases flush the WAL before acknowledging COMMIT, ensuring committed data survives crashes.

3. Consistency violated — NOT NULL constraint should prevent a NULL from being committed. A database enforcing consistency would roll back the transaction.

4. Non-repeatable read — this violates Isolation at the READ COMMITTED level. Transaction A sees a different value within its own transaction because Transaction B committed. Prevented by REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE isolation level.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Explain in your own words what a 'dirty read' is, why it is dangerous, and what isolation level prevents it.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
A dirty read occurs when Transaction A reads data that Transaction B has modified but not yet committed. If Transaction B then rolls back, Transaction A has read data that never officially existed — it made decisions based on phantom changes.

Danger: a booking system reads an 'available' status from an uncommitted insert that gets rolled back. It might show the seat as taken and refuse a valid booking.

Prevention: READ COMMITTED isolation level prevents dirty reads. At READ COMMITTED, a transaction can only see data that other transactions have already committed. It is the default isolation level in PostgreSQL and most production databases.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain each letter of ACID to someone who has never heard the term, using a real-world transaction (like a bank transfer) as your example.

options: Either all statements in a transaction succeed, or none of them do — no partial commits
All concurrent transactions see the same data simultaneously
All columns satisfy their constraints after every transaction
questions.answer: Either all statements in a transaction succeed, or none of them do — no partial commits
questions.explanation: Atomicity is the all-or-nothing property. If any part of a transaction fails, the engine rolls back the entire transaction, leaving the database in its pre-transaction state.

questions.prompt: Two concurrent transactions both read balance=500 and both intend to add 200. Each writes 700. What should the final balance be, and what ACID property prevents the wrong result?
options: 900 (correct) — Isolation prevents the lost update by using locking or optimistic concurrency
1400 — both transactions add 200 each so the total is 1400
questions.answer: 900 (correct) — Isolation prevents the lost update by using locking or optimistic concurrency
questions.explanation: Without isolation, both transactions read 500, add 200, and write 700 — the second write overwrites the first, losing 200. Proper isolation (row locking or SERIALIZABLE) serialises the transactions so the second reads the updated 700 and writes 900.

options: Reading uncommitted data from another transaction — data that may be rolled back
Reading data that has been deleted but not yet vacuumed
Reading a NULL value that should not exist
Reading a row that matches no index
questions.answer: Reading uncommitted data from another transaction — data that may be rolled back
questions.explanation: A dirty read occurs at READ UNCOMMITTED isolation. The reader sees changes that another transaction has not committed. If that transaction rolls back, the reader acted on data that never existed. READ COMMITTED and higher isolation levels prevent dirty reads.

questions.prompt: A NoSQL system offers eventual consistency instead of strong ACID guarantees. When is this acceptable?
options: When temporary inconsistency is acceptable — e.g. a social media like count that is off by a few for seconds before converging
When financial transactions must be reliable
When constraint enforcement (NOT NULL, FK) is required
When SELECT FOR UPDATE is needed
questions.answer: When temporary inconsistency is acceptable — e.g. a social media like count that is off by a few for seconds before converging
questions.explanation: Eventual consistency means replicas will converge to the same value eventually, but there is a window where different replicas show different data. Acceptable for counters, product descriptions, analytics. Not acceptable for account balances, inventory, or any use case where data correctness is immediately required.
